idiom_name: Double => Double (Function1) held by the context
implementation_notes: A strategy is a function value: the context takes a Double => Double (or any FunctionN), and the caller supplies a lambda, an eta-expanded method or a partially applied function; the collections API already works this way (map/filter take functions, sortBy a key function, sortWith a comparator function, sort(Ordering) an implicit one). The trait-plus-objects form is justified only when the strategy has state or several operations. The Scala 3 reference's contrast between ad-hoc polymorphism and plain function parameterisation is the rule of thumb: express the algorithm as a parameter until the type domain, not the call site, is what selects it.
pitfalls: A lambda is an allocated FunctionN instance (cached as a static only when it captures nothing), so strategies rebuilt inside a hot loop should be hoisted to a val or object.
Eta-expansion rules differ between Scala 2 and Scala 3: a bare method name may need an explicit underscore or type ascription before it can be a function value.

A function type carries no name or documentation, so a strategy chosen from configuration should be introduced through a named method, object or type alias, not an inline lambda at the selection site.

variants.name: Type-class instance selected by given/implicit resolution
variants.idiom_name: trait Ord[T] + given instance + using clause (the Ordering mechanism)
variants.implementation_notes: When the algorithm is a property of the data type rather than a per-call choice - an ordering, a serializer, a numeric tower - model it as a type class: a trait parameterised by the type, a given instance per type, and a method with a context parameter (def maximum[T](xs: List[T])(using ord: Ord[T])). The implementation is then supplied by implicit/given resolution instead of by an argument, which is how the standard library's Ordering drives sorted. Scala 3 syntax is given/using; Scala 2 spells the same design with implicit val and implicit parameters. This form trades runtime flexibility for composability: the choice is fixed at compile time by what is in scope.
pitfalls: Two instances of the same type in scope make the implicit search ambiguous - a compile error reported at the use site, far from the definitions; keep instances in the companion object and import alternatives deliberately.

Resolution is lexically scoped, so the algorithm actually chosen depends on what happens to be imported at the call site; where the choice matters, name the instance or pass it explicitly with (using ...).

Instances are resolved at compile time: swapping the algorithm at run time is not what this form is for, and a type class used as if it were a runtime strategy produces surprising rebinding behaviour.
